concepts.name: FDI vs FPI: Definitional Boundaries and Threshold Rule
key_dimensions: The 10% threshold rule: investment ≥10% of paid-up equity = FDI; <10% = FPI (FEMA classification)
UPSC trap: threshold applies to equity, not total capital — preference shares and debentures treated differently
Reclassification trigger: what happens when FPI crosses 10% limit — mandatory conversion to FDI route
Grey zone: strategic vs portfolio intent cannot always be inferred from percentage alone

concepts.name: Foreign Portfolio Investor (FPI) Regulatory Framework post-2019
key_dimensions: SEBI as the sole regulator for FPIs (replacing FII/QFI/sub-account categories merged in 2014, further refined 2019)
Three-category classification: Category I (government entities, central banks), Category II (regulated funds), Category III (all others) — differential KYC norms
UPSC trap: FIIs as a category no longer exist; SEBI replaced with FPI regime — older questions may still use FII terminology
Registration through Designated Depository Participants (DDPs), not directly with SEBI

concepts.name: FDI Policy Architecture: Automatic Route vs Government Route
key_dimensions: Automatic route: no prior government approval needed; sectors where RBI oversight suffices
Government route: approval through FIPB (abolished 2017) — now sector-specific ministries or DPIIT
UPSC trap: FIPB abolished in 2017 — questions may test whether students know the current approval mechanism
Prohibited sectors for FDI: lottery, gambling, chit funds, Nidhi companies, real estate business (not construction), tobacco manufacturing

concepts.name: Sectoral FDI Caps and Strategic Sensitivity
key_dimensions: 100% FDI allowed in most manufacturing, but caps in defence (74% auto route, beyond via government), insurance (74%), banking-private (74%), broadcasting (49–100% varies by segment)
Multi-brand retail: 51% cap with conditionalities (30% local sourcing, minimum investment $100 mn) — single brand retail 100%
UPSC trap: print media (26%) vs digital media (26% for news) vs entertainment (100%) — differentiated caps often tested
Strategic sectors where FDI is restricted vs prohibited: atomic energy (prohibited) vs defence (restricted)

concepts.name: FPI Investment Limits in Government and Corporate Bonds
key_dimensions: FPIs can invest in G-secs, T-bills, SDLs, corporate bonds — subject to macro-prudential limits set by RBI/SEBI
Voluntary Retention Route (VRR): FPIs commit to minimum 3-year retention in debt — exempted from macro-prudential limits
UPSC trap: FPIs cannot invest in unlisted corporate bonds below investment grade — often confused with general bond access
FAR (Fully Accessible Route): specific G-sec series open to non-resident investors without limits — key reform for Euroclear inclusion

concepts.name: Hot Money Problem and Macroeconomic Vulnerability
key_dimensions: FPI flows are reversible ('hot money') — sudden outflows cause exchange rate depreciation, equity market crash, reserve depletion
FDI considered 'stable' due to physical asset creation, but FPI provides liquidity and price discovery
Original Sin problem: India cannot borrow internationally in rupees, making FPI debt flows carry currency risk for investors
UPSC angle: 2013 Taper Tantrum, 2018 IL&FS crisis, 2020 COVID selloff — case studies in FPI-driven volatility

concepts.name: Transfer Pricing and Round-Tripping in FDI
key_dimensions: Round-tripping: Indian money routed through Mauritius/Singapore disguised as FDI to avoid taxes — exploits treaty shopping
GAAR (General Anti-Avoidance Rules, effective 2017) empowers tax authorities to deny treaty benefits if arrangement lacks commercial substance
Transfer pricing: manipulation of intra-company transaction prices between parent and subsidiary to shift profits to low-tax jurisdictions
UPSC trap: Mauritius was top FDI source for decades due to DTAA; post-2016 treaty revision, capital gains now taxable at source — shift in FDI geography

concepts.name: Participatory Notes (P-Notes) and Regulatory Concerns
key_dimensions: P-Notes (Offshore Derivative Instruments): FPIs issue these to foreign investors who don't want direct SEBI registration — underlying asset is Indian security
Anonymity concern: SEBI cannot identify ultimate beneficial owner (UBO) — used for money laundering and tax evasion allegations
Regulatory tightening: SEBI 2017 — P-Note issuance restricted, KYC on UBO mandatory, not allowed on derivatives without hedging purpose
UPSC trap: P-Note holders are NOT registered with SEBI — the FPI issuing P-Notes is registered, not the end investor

concepts.name: External Commercial Borrowings (ECB) vs FDI vs FPI: Overlaps
key_dimensions: ECB: loans raised by Indian entities from foreign sources — debt instrument, not equity; governed by RBI's ECB framework
FDI brings equity capital; ECB brings debt capital — both are foreign capital inflows but have different balance of payments treatment
UPSC trap: ECB repayment creates future current account pressure (interest + principal); FDI dividends are more flexible
Masala Bonds: rupee-denominated bonds issued overseas — hybrid between ECB and FPI debt; currency risk borne by investor

concepts.name: Balance of Payments Treatment: Capital Account vs Financial Account
key_dimensions: Post-BPM6: FDI and FPI recorded under Financial Account (not Capital Account as commonly misused in public discourse)
UPSC trap: 'Capital Account Convertibility' refers to freedom to convert rupee for capital transactions — India has partial CAC, not full
FDI inflows = credit in financial account; repatriation of FDI profits = debit in current account (under 'primary income')
Current account deficit (CAD) financing: FPI and FDI are key sources — sustainability analysis differs for each

concepts.name: FEMA vs FERA: Paradigm Shift in Foreign Investment Regulation
key_dimensions: FERA 1973: presumption of guilt, criminal prosecution for violations — reflected capital scarcity mindset
FEMA 1999: civil offence, presumption of innocence, liberalization mindset — ED enforcement for serious contraventions only
UPSC trap: FEMA violations are civil, not criminal (except money laundering which invokes PMLA separately)
Enforcement Directorate (ED) enforces both FEMA and PMLA — dual mandate often conflated in questions

concepts.name: Press Note 3 (2020) and Opportunistic FDI Restrictions
key_dimensions: Press Note 3 (2020): FDI from countries sharing land border with India (China, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan, Myanmar) requires government approval — no automatic route
Triggered by COVID-19 period concern about Chinese entities acquiring stressed Indian companies at depressed valuations
UPSC trap: applies to ALL sectors, not just sensitive ones — even sectors with 100% automatic route require government approval for land-border countries
Extends to beneficial ownership: if ultimate beneficial owner is from land-border country, same restriction applies even if immediate investor is from a third country

concepts.name: Qualified Foreign Investor (QFI) and Consolidation into FPI
key_dimensions: QFI introduced 2012 to allow direct retail foreign investor access to Indian equity and debt without going through FII route
Consolidated into FPI regime by SEBI in 2014 — QFI, FII, and sub-accounts merged into unified FPI category
UPSC trap: QFI no longer exists as a separate category — questions using older frameworks may mislead
Rationale for consolidation: regulatory arbitrage between categories was creating compliance gaps and investor confusion

concepts.name: Aggregate FPI Limit and Sectoral Investment Caps
key_dimensions: Aggregate FPI limit in a company: 24% of paid-up capital (can be increased to sectoral cap or statutory limit by board resolution)
Individual FPI limit: <10% of paid-up capital (beyond which reclassified as FDI)
UPSC trap: aggregate limit is a company-level decision; individual limit is regulatory — two different thresholds operating simultaneously
Once aggregate FPI limit is breached, subsequent FPI purchases trigger automatic divestment — 'creeping acquisition' parallel with SEBI Takeover Code

concepts.name: Sovereign Wealth Funds (SWFs) and Their Regulatory Treatment
key_dimensions: SWFs are state-owned investment funds — classified as Category I FPI under SEBI framework
Tax treatment: Union Budget 2020 exempted SWFs and pension funds from tax on interest, dividend, and capital gains for infrastructure investments with 3-year lock-in
UPSC angle: SWFs represent quasi-FDI (strategic long-term) but regulated as FPI — creates policy ambiguity
Geopolitical dimension: investments from state-controlled SWFs raise national security concerns similar to Press Note 3 logic

concepts.name: Impact of FDI on Current Account Deficit and Rupee Stability
key_dimensions: FDI initially improves capital account; over time, profit repatriation worsens current account — lifecycle effect
FPI in equity: dividend repatriation hits current account; capital gains repatriation hits financial account
UPSC trap: all foreign investment eventually creates outflow obligations — quality of FDI (export-oriented vs domestic market) determines net current account impact
RBI uses forex reserves (partly built from FPI/FDI flows) to stabilize rupee during sudden reversals — reserve adequacy metrics

concepts.name: National Investment and Infrastructure Fund (NIIF) as Quasi-FDI Vehicle
key_dimensions: NIIF: government-owned fund designed to attract long-term foreign capital into Indian infrastructure — acts as intermediary
Structure: Master Fund, Fund of Funds, Strategic Opportunities Fund — different risk-return profiles
UPSC trap: NIIF is not a sovereign wealth fund (government owns 49%, rest is private/foreign) — often confused with SWF
Distinction from FDI: NIIF investment is pooled with government capital — blended finance model to de-risk foreign investors

concepts.name: Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs) and InvITs as FPI Entry Points
key_dimensions: REITs and InvITs listed on stock exchanges — FPIs can invest in units, giving real estate/infrastructure exposure without direct FDI
UPSC trap: FDI in 'real estate business' is prohibited, but FDI in construction development and investment via REITs is permitted — critical distinction
Minimum 80% of assets must be revenue-generating (completed) assets in REIT — prevents speculative construction exposure
InvIT: infrastructure assets (roads, power transmission, pipelines) — NHAI and PowerGrid have listed InvITs as monetization tool

concepts.name: Double Taxation Avoidance Agreements (DTAAs) and FDI Geography
key_dimensions: DTAA determines where capital gains are taxed — source country (India) or residence country (investor's home)
Mauritius DTAA (pre-2016): capital gains taxable only in Mauritius (which didn't tax them) — made Mauritius top FDI source; revised 2016 to tax at source
Singapore DTAA: grandfathering provision protected investments made before April 2017 — sunset clause design
UPSC trap: after DTAA renegotiations, Netherlands and USA have become larger FDI sources — geography of FDI inflows shifted post-2017

concepts.name: Foreign Investment Facilitation Portal (FIFP) and DPIIT's Role Post-FIPB Abolition
key_dimensions: FIPB abolished May 2017 — government route approvals now handled by competent sectoral ministries with DPIIT as facilitator
FIFP: single online window for FDI applications requiring government approval — DPIIT routes applications to respective ministries
UPSC trap: DPIIT does NOT approve FDI directly (except in its own sector) — it facilitates, coordinates and maintains FDI data
Time limit for approval: 8-10 weeks from receipt of complete application — missed deadlines treated as deemed approval in some frameworks
